text: In February 2011, David Heath saw a Facebook post noting that socks are the number one most-requested clothing item at homeless shelters. He shared it with Randy Goldberg, and the two started buying and handing out socks before turning it into a buy-one-give-one business, modeled loosely on TOMS and Warby Parker.
Heath and Goldberg met while both working at the same media company, Goldberg ran the editorial department, Heath worked in sales, after each had already tried side businesses of their own.

Randy Goldberg graduated from Georgetown with a finance degree, was laid off from a consulting job within seven months due to a recession, then worked odd jobs, including waiting tables and a wine shop, before moving into advertising and branding.
David Heath has cited his father's playground-surfacing business, which he watched grow over 35 years, as an early influence on his entrepreneurial mindset.

evidence.quote: I watched him grow it over 35 years

notes: Article published 2025-01-06. Speaker: David Heath, co-founder and CEO.

text: On Shark Tank, other sharks warned that the buy-one-give-one model would hurt margins, but Heath and Goldberg picked Daymond John's offer because, in their telling, he understood the mission.
notes: Article published 2023-10-30. This is the article's paraphrase, not a verbatim quote from the founders.

text: Heath and Goldberg have said Bombas deliberately avoided rapid venture-fueled scaling, building the company year over year rather than racing to be the biggest brand quickly, comparing the approach to Nike and Patagonia.
Randy Goldberg, co-founder, on deciding to start the business with Heath while both had full-time jobs elsewhere.

evidence.quote: We realized we both had a passion for entrepreneurship and wanted to start our own business someday. We were working full-time, and then also working on the side.

text: David Heath, co-founder and CEO, describing the profitable, patient model he wanted Bombas to emulate rather than pursuing rapid VC-funded growth.

evidence.quote: They were always profitable from day one; they built these businesses brick by brick over many years

text: David Heath, co-founder and CEO, on choosing not to chase a large venture raise to grow as fast as possible.

evidence.quote: We were never the brand that was like let's go out and raise $150 million and try to be the biggest company as quickly as possible.

text: David Heath, co-founder and CEO, on investing heavily in brand from the start.

evidence.quote: From day one, as part of our go-to-market strategy, we invested heavily in brand.

text: Randy Goldberg, co-founder, on the core giving model and why socks were the starting product: the most-requested item at homeless shelters.

evidence.quote: We donate a product for every product we sell

text: Randy Goldberg, co-founder, on why socks, underwear and t-shirts are treated as the core product line: they are the things you put on first in the morning, which demands careful design.

evidence.quote: the things that you put on first in the morning

text: Randy Goldberg, co-founder, on why the items closest to the body have the biggest impact on comfort, used to explain the bralette launch.

evidence.quote: The first things that you put on in the morning and take off at night, they're having the biggest impact on your comfort.

text: Bombas pitched on Shark Tank in the Season 6 premiere, which first aired September 26, 2014, and closed a deal with Daymond John of $200,000 for 17.5 percent equity.
notes: Deal terms and Daymond John's involvement confirmed directly by CNBC (published 2017-08-21); episode air date confirmed via IMDb episode record.

text: Bombas set an original goal of donating 1 million pairs of socks within 10 years of founding, and reached that milestone in about two and a half years, around 2016.
notes: Year is an estimate derived from the stated pace, not a date stamped on the source page.

text: Bombas reached 10 million pairs and items donated within about five years of its 2013 founding; a campaign marking the 10 millionth pair ran around November 2018.
notes: Campaign coverage dated November 2018; exact day not given.

text: As of a November 2021 interview, Bombas had donated and sold over 45 million items to date, working with more than 3,500 Giving Partners across all 50 states.
As of June 2022, Bombas had distributed over 86 million clothing items through about 3,500 Giving Partners.
notes: Reported retrospectively in a March 2023 article referencing the June 2022 figure.

text: Bombas donated its 100 millionth item in 2023, its tenth year in business, marked with a mission-driven Compassion Campaign rather than self-promotion; the Giving Partner network stood at more than 3,500 at the time.
notes: Company page dated to 2023; exact day not given.
